source.title: The Prince
source.attribution: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (trans. W. K. Marriott), Standard Ebooks, public domain
source.notes: Cards draw only on the book's advice about advisers, preparation, change and learning; its endorsements of cruelty and deceit are deliberately left out.

cards.title: People judge a leader by the team they choose
cards.body:
Machiavelli said the first thing people notice about a ruler is the people around him. Capable, loyal staff signal good judgment; weak or self-serving ones reveal a poor eye for character.

This holds for any manager or founder. Your hires and closest collaborators are a public record of your judgment, and they shape what gets done when you are not in the room. Hiring carefully, recognising real ability and treating good people well enough that they stay is not a side task of leadership; it is much of the job.
cards.quote: And the first opinion which one forms of a prince, and of his understanding, is by observing the men he has around him; and when they are capable and faithful he may always be considered wise
cards.locator: XXII. Concerning the Secretaries of Princes ¶1
cards.apply_it: Look at the people you rely on most at work. What does that group say about your judgment, and is there one gap you should fill?

quiz.question: According to Machiavelli, how do people first judge a ruler's understanding?
options: By his speeches
By the people he keeps around him
By the size of his army
By his family name
quiz.explanation: Capable, faithful advisers show that the ruler knows how to recognise ability and keep it.

cards.title: Make it safe for people to tell you the truth
cards.body:
Machiavelli saw flattery as one of the biggest dangers to anyone in charge. Leaders like hearing that their plans are good, and staff quickly learn to say so. The only real defence is to show that honest answers will never be punished.

He also advised asking good advisers about everything, listening patiently, and then making your own decision. In a modern team that means inviting critique before a launch, thanking the person who points out the flaw, and still owning the final call rather than drifting with whoever spoke last.
cards.quote: there is no other way of guarding oneself from flatterers except letting men understand that to tell you the truth does not offend you
cards.locator: XXIII. How Flatterers Should Be Avoided ¶1
cards.apply_it: In your next meeting, ask directly: what is the weakest part of this plan? Then thank whoever answers honestly.

quiz.question: What did Machiavelli see as the only real guard against flatterers?
options: Letting people know the truth does not offend you
Hiring fewer advisers
Ignoring all advice
Making decisions in secret
quiz.explanation: If people know honesty is safe, they stop telling you only what you want to hear.

cards.title: Expect resistance when you introduce something new
cards.body:
Machiavelli called leading change one of the hardest and riskiest things to attempt. Those who did well under the old way will oppose you openly, while those who might gain from the new way support you only half-heartedly, because they have not yet seen it work.

Anyone rolling out a new process, tool or strategy meets this pattern. Plan for it: explain the reasons, show early wins quickly, and address what people stand to lose. Treat lukewarm support as normal rather than a sign the idea is wrong.
cards.quote: there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things
cards.locator: VI. Concerning New Principalities Which Are… ¶5
cards.apply_it: For a change you want to make, list who loses something under it and one thing you can do to address their concern.

quiz.question: Why, according to Machiavelli, do new ways of doing things get only lukewarm support?
options: People do not believe in new things until they have long experience of them
New ideas are usually bad
Leaders rarely explain them
Supporters are always paid by rivals
quiz.explanation: Potential winners hesitate because they have not yet seen the new order work, while those who did well under the old one resist.

cards.title: Build the flood barriers while the weather is calm
cards.body:
Machiavelli compared luck to a river that floods and sweeps everything away. You cannot stop the flood, but in calm weather you can build banks and channels so that when it comes the damage is limited. Fortune, he wrote, hits hardest where nobody prepared.

For a business or a household, the calm stretch is when to build an emergency fund, back up data, diversify clients and write the contingency plan. Waiting until the crisis arrives means making every decision in a panic.
cards.quote: So it happens with fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her.
cards.locator: XXV. What Fortune Can Effect in Human… ¶2
cards.apply_it: While things are calm, pick one risk you face and take one step to soften it, such as a backup, a buffer or a second option.

quiz.question: In Machiavelli's river image, when should defences be built?
options: During the flood
Only after the first disaster
Never; floods cannot be resisted
When the weather is fair
quiz.explanation: Defences have to be raised in calm times so the next flood does less damage.

cards.title: Study the best in your field and aim a little higher than you need
cards.body:
Machiavelli advised learning from the most outstanding people who came before you. Even if you never match them, some of their quality rubs off. He compared this to skilled archers who aim above a distant target, knowing the arrow will drop.

Today that might mean reading how great founders, managers or craftspeople actually worked, and setting goals slightly beyond what feels comfortable. Aiming high, while being honest about your current range, tends to land you further than aiming only at what you are sure you can reach.
cards.quote: A wise man ought always to follow the paths beaten by great men, and to imitate those who have been supreme, so that if his ability does not equal theirs, at least it will savour of it.
cards.locator: VI. Concerning New Principalities Which Are… ¶1
cards.apply_it: Choose one person who is excellent at what you do. Find one specific habit of theirs and try it this week.

quiz.question: Why did Machiavelli's clever archers aim higher than the mark?
options: To impress onlookers
Because the target was moving
So the arrow, falling short of the high aim, would still hit the target
To test a new bow
quiz.explanation: Knowing their limits, they aimed high so that their shot would still reach the mark.

cards.title: Fix problems while they are small, before they become obvious
cards.body:
Machiavelli borrows a doctor's observation: some illnesses are easy to cure at the start but hard to spot, and later easy to spot but hard to cure. He argues that troubles in public life work the same way. The wise leader notices them early and acts while the fix is still cheap.

This applies to a leaking roof, a small debt, a tense silence with a colleague or a customer who has gone quiet. By the time everyone can see the problem, your options have shrunk. Paying attention to faint early signals is one of the most valuable habits you can build.
cards.quote: in the beginning of the malady it is easy to cure but difficult to detect, but in the course of time... it becomes easy to detect but difficult to cure.
cards.locator: III. Concerning Mixed Principalities ¶10
cards.apply_it: Name one small problem you have been ignoring because it is not urgent yet. Spend 15 minutes on it today.

quiz.question: According to the hectic fever comparison, when is a problem easiest to fix?
options: Once everyone can clearly see it
After it has peaked and started to fade
At the start, when it is still hard to notice
Only when an expert is called in
quiz.explanation: Machiavelli says early problems are easy to cure but hard to detect; waiting makes them obvious but hard to fix.

cards.title: Stay close to the work so you hear about problems early
cards.body:
Machiavelli notes that a ruler who lives in the territory he governs sees disorder as it starts and can deal with it quickly. One who stays far away only hears about trouble once it has grown too big to handle.

The same is true of managers, business owners and parents. If you only learn what is happening through reports, you learn late. Walking the shop floor, visiting the branch, or simply asking the people doing the work how things are going gives you the early warning that distance takes away.
cards.quote: if one is on the spot, disorders are seen as they spring up, and one can quickly remedy them; but if one is not at hand, they are heard of only when they are great
cards.locator: III. Concerning Mixed Principalities ¶6
cards.apply_it: This week, spend one hour where the real work happens in your business or team, and just watch and ask questions.

quiz.question: Why does Machiavelli advise a ruler to live in the territory he governs?
options: So he can collect more taxes personally
So he can avoid his advisers
So he looks humble to foreign powers
So he can spot and fix disorder as soon as it starts
quiz.explanation: Being on the spot means troubles are seen as they spring up, while distance means hearing of them only when they are too big.

cards.title: Avoiding a hard conversation usually just postpones it on worse terms
cards.body:
Machiavelli criticises King Louis XII for making a bad concession to dodge a war. His point: a conflict that is coming cannot really be avoided by a blunder; it is only delayed, and the delay usually favours the other side.

In everyday life we often give ground, stay silent or agree to bad terms just to keep the peace for now. Sometimes that is wise. But if the disagreement is real, avoiding it tends to let it grow and weakens your position. Facing it early, calmly and honestly is often the kinder and safer choice.
cards.quote: a blunder ought never to be perpetrated to avoid war, because it is not to be avoided, but is only deferred to your disadvantage.
cards.locator: III. Concerning Mixed Principalities ¶17
cards.apply_it: Think of a conversation you keep putting off. Write down the first sentence you would say, and set a date to have it.

quiz.question: What does Machiavelli say happens when you make a bad concession just to avoid a conflict?
options: The conflict is only delayed, usually to your disadvantage
The conflict disappears for good
The other side becomes your loyal friend
You gain a reputation for strength
quiz.explanation: He argues the conflict is not avoided, only deferred, and the delay works against you.

cards.title: Be careful when you help someone else become far more powerful
cards.body:
Looking at how France helped the Church and Spain grow strong in Italy, only to be pushed out by them, Machiavelli draws a blunt rule: whoever makes another powerful often ends up ruined by them. The newly powerful party tends to distrust the very skill or strength that lifted it.

This is not a reason to stop helping people. It is a reminder to protect yourself when you hand over key customers, skills, money or control. Get agreements in writing, keep some independence, and don't assume gratitude will last once the balance of power shifts.
cards.quote: he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined
cards.locator: III. Concerning Mixed Principalities ¶18
cards.apply_it: Is there a partner, client or relative you are helping grow? Write down one safeguard that keeps you from becoming fully dependent on them.

quiz.question: What warning does Machiavelli draw from France's dealings in Italy?
options: Helping allies always guarantees their loyalty
Making another party powerful can lead to your own ruin
Small states should never form alliances
Wars are won by having many weak friends
quiz.explanation: France helped the Church and Spain grow strong, and they later drove France out. He turns this into a general warning.

cards.title: Sudden success needs foundations built quickly afterwards
cards.body:
Machiavelli observes that rulers who rise suddenly, by luck or someone else's favour, have an easy climb but a hard time staying on top. Like plants that shoot up fast, they have shallow roots, and the first storm can knock them down unless they quickly lay the foundations others built slowly.

Today this fits a sudden promotion, a viral product, an inheritance or a big contract. The windfall is the start, not the finish. Use the good moment to learn the skills, build the systems, savings and relationships that would have come with slower growth.
cards.quote: States that rise unexpectedly, then, like all other things in nature which are born and grow rapidly, cannot leave their foundations and correspondencies fixed in such a way that the first storm will not overthrow them
cards.locator: VII. Concerning New Principalities Which Are… ¶2
cards.apply_it: If something good came to you quickly (a role, money, attention), list two foundations you still need to build to keep it.

quiz.question: What is the main risk for those who rise suddenly through luck?
options: They have too many loyal supporters
They become too cautious to act
They lack the foundations to survive the first storm
They are forced to give their gains away
quiz.explanation: Like fast-growing plants, sudden risers have shallow roots and must quickly lay the foundations others built over time.

cards.title: Don't assume new favours wipe out old hurts
cards.body:
Machiavelli says Cesare Borgia's fatal mistake was backing a man he had once wronged for the papacy, trusting that new benefits would make him forget. They didn't. Machiavelli concludes that people who have been hurt by you, or fear you, rarely let it go just because you are kind to them now.

The practical lesson is protective, not cynical: if you have harmed someone, a gift or favour is not the same as repair. Acknowledge the hurt honestly. And before you depend on someone, ask whether there is an old injury between you that has never really been settled.
cards.quote: He who believes that new benefits will cause great personages to forget old injuries is deceived.
cards.locator: VII. Concerning New Principalities Which Are… ¶12
cards.apply_it: Is there someone you once wronged and tried to make up for with favours? Consider a sincere, direct apology instead.

quiz.question: What was Cesare Borgia's mistake, according to Machiavelli?
options: Spending too much money on his army
Refusing to take any advice
Moving his court too far from Rome
Trusting that new benefits would make a man forget old injuries
quiz.explanation: He supported someone he had injured, believing new benefits would erase old grievances, and it led to his ruin.

cards.title: Deliver unavoidable bad news at once, and spread good news over time
cards.body:
Writing about how new rulers handle harsh measures, Machiavelli makes a psychological point: pain delivered in one go is felt less than pain repeated again and again, while rewards given little by little keep their pleasant effect longer.

At work this is a useful guide for decent leadership. If a restructure, budget cut or difficult change must happen, do it clearly and completely, rather than in many small shocks that keep people anxious. Rewards and recognition, on the other hand, land better when they come regularly rather than in one big burst that is soon forgotten.
cards.quote: injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.
cards.locator: VIII. Concerning Those Who Have Obtained a… ¶7
cards.apply_it: If you must deliver hard news, put it all in one honest message. Then plan small, regular thank-yous rather than one big gesture.

quiz.question: How does Machiavelli suggest handling unavoidable hardships and rewards?
options: Hardships all at once, rewards little by little
Hardships slowly, rewards all at once
Both slowly over many years
Both all at once at the start
quiz.explanation: Pain given at once is felt less; benefits given gradually keep their flavour longer.

cards.title: Be steady in good times, because last-minute changes earn no credit
cards.body:
Machiavelli advises living in a way that no sudden change of fortune forces you to transform overnight. If you only become generous, fair or strict when a crisis hits, it is too late: harsh steps fail, and kind ones look forced, so nobody feels thankful for them.

Think of a boss who starts praising staff only when they threaten to quit, or a partner who changes only when the relationship is ending. Consistent character built in ordinary times is what people trust when things go wrong.
cards.quote: mild ones will not help you, for they will be considered as forced from you, and no one will be under any obligation to you for them.
cards.locator: VIII. Concerning Those Who Have Obtained a… ¶8
cards.apply_it: Pick one good behaviour you tend to save for emergencies (thanking people, checking in, saving) and do it this week while things are calm.

quiz.question: Why do kind measures taken in a crisis often fail, according to Machiavelli?
options: They are too expensive to keep up
People see them as forced, so they feel no obligation
People prefer harsh measures in a crisis
They are never announced publicly
quiz.explanation: Changes made under pressure look forced, so nobody feels grateful or obligated for them.

cards.title: Most people simply want not to be mistreated, and that is easy to give
cards.body:
Machiavelli contrasts the powerful few, who want to dominate, with ordinary people, who mainly want not to be oppressed. He argues the second group's wish is fairer and far easier to satisfy, and that a leader backed by the many is more secure than one relying on a small elite.

In a company or community, this means your strongest base is usually the broad group of ordinary members, staff or customers. You don't win them with flashy perks. You win them by treating them fairly, keeping promises and not abusing your position.
cards.quote: their object is more righteous than that of the nobles, the latter wishing to oppress, while the former only desire not to be oppressed.
cards.locator: IX. Concerning a Civil Principality ¶3
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: is there any way people below you might feel pushed around? Fix one of those things this month.

quiz.question: According to Machiavelli, what do ordinary people mainly want from those in power?
options: Expensive gifts and festivals
A share in ruling
Not to be oppressed
Constant change and excitement
quiz.explanation: He says the people only desire not to be oppressed, which is fairer and easier to satisfy than the ambitions of the few.

cards.title: Good treatment from someone you expected harm from earns deep loyalty
cards.body:
Machiavelli notes that when people receive good from someone they expected to treat them badly, they become more attached to that person than if they had liked him from the start.

This is a hopeful idea for anyone starting out on the wrong foot: a new manager people are nervous about, an in-law who was not welcomed, a business that once let customers down. Fair, generous treatment that surprises people can turn suspicion into strong loyalty. First impressions matter, but what you do next can matter more.
cards.quote: men, when they receive good from him of whom they were expecting evil, are bound more closely to their benefactor
cards.locator: IX. Concerning a Civil Principality ¶5
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who is wary of you. What is one fair or generous thing you could do that would surprise them?

quiz.question: What happens when people receive good from someone they expected harm from?
options: They become even more suspicious
They forget the person quickly
They demand even more favours
They become more closely bound to that person
quiz.explanation: Machiavelli says unexpected good treatment binds people more closely than favour they already expected.

cards.title: Keep enough reserves to outlast a long siege
cards.body:
Machiavelli admired the free German cities of his day. They were hard to attack partly because they kept a full year's supply of food, drink and fuel in public stores, and always had work to keep people earning. Attackers knew a siege would be long and costly, so they rarely tried.

Your household can use the same idea. An emergency fund, a little food stored, and skills that can earn an income make you far less vulnerable to job loss, illness or rising prices. Reserves don't just help in a crisis; they give you the calm to make better decisions.
cards.quote: they always keep in public depots enough for one year's eating, drinking, and firing.
cards.locator: X. Concerning the Way in Which the… ¶2
cards.apply_it: Work out how many weeks your household could cover basic costs with no income. Set a small monthly amount to grow that number.

quiz.question: What made the free German cities hard to attack, in part?
options: They kept a year's supply of food, drink and fuel
They paid large bribes to neighbours
They had no walls, so nothing to attack
They relied on foreign armies
quiz.explanation: Their stored supplies and steady work meant a siege would be long and costly, discouraging attackers.

cards.title: People grow attached to those they have helped, not only those who help them
cards.body:
Machiavelli notices something surprising about human nature: we become bound to people not just by the favours we receive from them but also by the favours we do for them. Having sacrificed for a cause or a leader, people feel more committed to it.

You can use this kindly. Inviting a new colleague to help you, asking a neighbour for advice, or letting a friend contribute to your project can deepen the relationship. People value what they have invested in, so giving others a real chance to contribute builds connection.
cards.quote: it is the nature of men to be bound by the benefits they confer as much as by those they receive.
cards.locator: X. Concerning the Way in Which the… ¶4
cards.apply_it: Ask someone you would like to know better for a small piece of help or advice, and thank them properly afterwards.

quiz.question: What does Machiavelli say binds people to one another?
options: Only the gifts they receive
The benefits they give as much as the benefits they receive
Only fear of punishment
Only shared family ties
quiz.explanation: He says people are bound by the benefits they confer as much as by those they receive.

cards.title: Build your own strength instead of relying on borrowed power
cards.body:
After chapters on hired and borrowed armies, Machiavelli concludes that no state is safe without its own forces. Power that rests on someone else's strength depends entirely on luck and can vanish when that support is withdrawn.

For an individual, your 'own forces' are your skills, savings, reputation and relationships. A job title, a rich relative or a single big client can disappear. Investing steadily in abilities and resources that belong to you is what keeps you standing when outside support falls away.
cards.quote: nothing can be so uncertain or unstable as fame or power not founded on its own strength.
cards.locator: XIII. Concerning Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery,… ¶11
cards.apply_it: List what your income or position depends on. Pick one item you do not control and start building a backup you do control.

quiz.question: What does Machiavelli say about power not founded on its own strength?
options: It is the safest kind of power
It lasts longer than earned power
It is the most uncertain and unstable kind
It is only a problem in peacetime
quiz.explanation: He says nothing is as uncertain or unstable as fame or power not founded on its own strength.

cards.title: Use tools and methods that fit you, not someone else's armour
cards.body:
Machiavelli recalls the story of David, who was given King Saul's armour before facing Goliath. David took it off at once, saying he could not use it, and went out with his own sling and knife. Machiavelli concludes that other people's weapons either fall off you, weigh you down or tie you up.

Today we are offered endless borrowed systems: a famous CEO's morning routine, a friend's business model, an app everyone praises. Some help, but many simply don't fit. Prefer the methods you can actually handle well, even if they look humbler.
cards.quote: the arms of others either fall from your back, or they weigh you down, or they bind you fast.
cards.locator: XIII. Concerning Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery,… ¶8
cards.apply_it: Think of a method or routine you adopted because someone else swore by it. Is it helping you? Keep, adapt or drop it this week.

quiz.question: Why did David reject Saul's armour in Machiavelli's example?
options: It was too valuable to risk in battle
Saul asked for it back
He wanted to look braver without it
He could make no use of it and preferred his own sling and knife
quiz.explanation: David said he could not use the borrowed armour and chose to fight with the weapons he knew.

cards.title: Beware rescuers who become your masters
cards.body:
Machiavelli warns about calling in a powerful outside force to fight for you. If it loses, you are ruined with it; if it wins, you are now in its power.

In business and personal life this applies to a big investor who rescues a struggling firm, a lender who bails you out, or a powerful patron who solves your problem. Help like this can be useful, but count the cost: what control or freedom are you handing over? Wherever possible, accept help on terms that leave you able to stand on your own afterwards.
cards.quote: for losing, one is undone, and winning, one is their captive.
cards.locator: XIII. Concerning Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery,… ¶1
cards.apply_it: Before accepting a large loan, investor or favour, write down what control you would give up and whether you could exit later.

quiz.question: What is the danger of relying on a powerful outside force, according to Machiavelli?
options: If it loses you are ruined, and if it wins you are in its power
It always switches sides immediately
It costs nothing but achieves little
It makes your own team lazy but safe
quiz.explanation: With borrowed forces, losing undoes you and winning leaves you their captive.

cards.title: Look for the hidden poison in deals that look great at first
cards.body:
Machiavelli says people often enter an arrangement that looks attractive at the start without seeing the poison hidden inside it. He gives the example of Rome hiring Gothic soldiers, a step that seemed useful but began the empire's decline. True wisdom, he says, is recognising harm before it arrives, and few people manage it.

Offers that look very good, like easy credit, a quick-profit scheme or a too-generous partnership, deserve a second look. Ask what could go wrong in a year or five years, not just what you gain this week.
cards.quote: the scanty wisdom of man, on entering into an affair which looks well at first, cannot discern the poison that is hidden in it
cards.locator: XIII. Concerning Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery,… ¶10
cards.apply_it: For the next attractive offer you get, write down three ways it could hurt you later before you say yes.

quiz.question: What does Machiavelli say people often miss when entering an affair that looks good at first?
options: The paperwork it requires
The poison hidden inside it
The friends they could invite
The quick rewards it offers
quiz.explanation: He warns that limited human wisdom often fails to see the poison hidden in deals that look attractive at first.

cards.title: Rehearse 'what if' scenarios in calm times
cards.body:
Machiavelli praises Philopoemen, a Greek leader who, even on country walks with friends in peacetime, would stop and ask: if an enemy were on that hill, what should we do? He would argue it out, listen to their views and give his own reasons. As a result, when war came, very little could surprise him.

You can do the same for the risks in your life and work. What if a key customer leaves? What if the power goes off on launch day? Talking through scenarios in advance turns panic into a plan.
cards.quote: by these continual discussions there could never arise, in time of war, any unexpected circumstances that he could not deal with.
cards.locator: XIV. That Which Concerns a Prince on the… ¶3
cards.apply_it: Pick one likely setback in your work or home. With a friend or colleague, talk through what you'd do in the first 24 hours.

quiz.question: What did Philopoemen do in peacetime that Machiavelli admired?
options: Rested completely from all thoughts of war
Hired foreign generals to plan for him
Discussed 'what if' battle scenarios with his friends
Avoided travelling in the countryside
quiz.explanation: He constantly discussed possible situations, so nothing unexpected could catch him unprepared.

cards.title: Study why others failed as closely as why they succeeded
cards.body:
Machiavelli advises reading the lives of notable people and examining the causes of both their victories and their defeats, so you can imitate the first and avoid the second. He adds that the wise never sit idle in good times but build up resources they can use when fortune turns.

Most of us study success stories only. Yet failures often teach more clearly, and cost you nothing if they are someone else's. When you read a biography or watch a business collapse, ask what caused it and how you would avoid it.
cards.quote: to examine the causes of their victories and defeat, so as to avoid the latter and imitate the former
cards.locator: XIV. That Which Concerns a Prince on the… ¶4
cards.apply_it: Pick a business or person whose failure you know about. Write down two causes and one way to avoid each in your own life.

quiz.question: What does Machiavelli advise studying in the lives of great people?
options: Only their victories
Only their family background
Only their public speeches
The causes of both their victories and their defeats
quiz.explanation: He says to examine the causes of both, imitating the victories and avoiding the defeats.

cards.title: Know one area deeply and you will learn others faster
cards.body:
Machiavelli tells rulers to know their own land in detail: how hills rise, valleys open and rivers run. He points out a second benefit. Because landscapes resemble each other, someone who understands one region can quickly understand any other.

The principle reaches well beyond terrain. Deep knowledge of one market, one craft or one subject gives you patterns you can recognise elsewhere. A person who has truly mastered running one small shop learns a second business far faster than someone who has only skimmed many.
cards.quote: with a knowledge of the aspect of one country one can easily arrive at a knowledge of others.
cards.locator: XIV. That Which Concerns a Prince on the… ¶2
cards.apply_it: Choose one area of your work to understand thoroughly this month. Note one pattern from it that could apply elsewhere.

quiz.question: Why does Machiavelli say knowing your own land well also helps elsewhere?
options: Landscapes resemble each other, so knowledge transfers
Other countries are always identical
Enemies never travel to new places
It lets you avoid learning anything new
quiz.explanation: Because one region resembles others, deep knowledge of one helps you understand others easily.

cards.title: Plan for the world as it is, not as it ought to be
cards.body:
Machiavelli says many writers described ideal states that never existed. He chose instead to write about how people actually behave, because the gap between how we live and how we ought to live is huge, and ignoring it leads to ruin.

You can hold high values and still be realistic. Assume some people will pay late, some promises will be broken and some plans will slip. Building your budget, contracts and expectations around real behaviour, rather than ideal behaviour, protects you and the people who rely on you.
cards.quote: how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation
cards.locator: XV. Concerning Things for Which Men, and… ¶1
cards.apply_it: Look at one plan you are making. Where have you assumed people will behave perfectly? Add a buffer for real-world behaviour.

quiz.question: Why did Machiavelli choose to write about how people actually behave?
options: He believed ideals do not matter at all
Ignoring how people really act leads to ruin
He had never read other writers
He wanted to describe imaginary republics
quiz.explanation: He says the gap between how we live and how we ought to live is so large that ignoring it brings ruin.

cards.title: Showy generosity can drain you faster than anything
cards.body:
Machiavelli warns that nothing runs out as quickly as lavish giving done for reputation. While you spend to look generous, you lose the means to keep doing it, and end up either poor or forced to squeeze others to keep up appearances.

This is a real trap: big weddings, rounds of drinks, gifts and loans we can't afford, given so people think well of us. Real generosity is sustainable. Give what you can keep giving, and don't let the wish to look rich make you poor.
cards.quote: there is nothing wastes so rapidly as liberality, for even whilst you exercise it you lose the power to do so
cards.locator: XVI. Concerning Liberality and Meanness ¶5
cards.apply_it: Set a monthly limit for gifts, contributions and treats for others, and stick to it even when you feel pressure to impress.

quiz.question: What problem does Machiavelli see with lavish generosity done for reputation?
options: It always makes people grateful forever
It costs nothing in the long run
It drains your means so you soon cannot keep it up
It is the fastest way to build wealth
quiz.explanation: He says it wastes faster than anything: while giving lavishly you lose the power to keep giving.

cards.title: Quiet thrift pays for the big moves later
cards.body:
Machiavelli points out that Pope Julius II fought costly campaigns without imposing extra taxes, because he had built up money through long thriftiness. Being seen as careful with money, he argues, is a small price compared with the freedom it gives to act.

People may call you tight when you skip expensive outings or keep driving an old car. But steady saving is what lets you start a business, pay for training, or handle an emergency without borrowing. A modest reputation for carefulness is worth the options it buys.
cards.quote: he supplied his additional expenses out of his long thriftiness.
cards.locator: XVI. Concerning Liberality and Meanness ¶3
cards.apply_it: Pick one regular expense you mostly keep up for appearances. Cut it and move the money into savings for a future goal.

quiz.question: How did Pope Julius II pay for his campaigns without new taxes?
options: By borrowing from foreign banks
By selling Church land
By cutting his army in half
From money saved through long thriftiness
quiz.explanation: Machiavelli says he covered his additional expenses out of his long thriftiness.

cards.title: Balance trust and caution: neither naive nor paranoid
cards.body:
Machiavelli advises being slow to believe and slow to act, avoiding showing fear, and moving with prudence and humanity. Too much confidence makes you careless; too much distrust makes you impossible to live with.

This balance matters in every relationship and workplace. Checking facts before reacting to gossip, or reading a contract before signing, is wise. But treating everyone as a suspect drives good people away. Aim for calm, reasonable trust that you adjust based on evidence.
cards.quote: too much confidence may not make him incautious and too much distrust render him intolerable.
cards.locator: XVII. Concerning Cruelty and Clemency, and… ¶4
cards.apply_it: Next time you hear something alarming about someone, wait and check one fact before you react or repeat it.

quiz.question: What two extremes does Machiavelli warn against?
options: Too much confidence and too much distrust
Too much reading and too little sleep
Too much travel and too little rest
Too much praise and too little criticism
quiz.explanation: He warns that overconfidence makes you careless and excessive distrust makes you intolerable.

cards.title: Never mess with people's livelihood
cards.body:
Machiavelli observes that rulers become hated above all when they take people's property. He makes the striking claim that people forget even the death of a father more quickly than the loss of their inheritance.

Whatever you think of that exaggeration, the lesson for leaders is clear: nothing destroys goodwill faster than touching people's income or possessions unfairly. Late wages, unexplained deductions, or taking credit for someone's work cause deep, lasting resentment. Protect people's earnings, and they will forgive many other mistakes.
cards.quote: men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony.
cards.locator: XVII. Concerning Cruelty and Clemency, and… ¶6
cards.apply_it: If you manage or pay anyone, check that every payment is on time and explained clearly this month.

quiz.question: What does Machiavelli say most quickly makes a ruler hated?
options: Holding public festivals
Taking people's property
Asking for advice
Living in the territory he rules
quiz.explanation: He says rulers must keep their hands off people’s property, since its loss is resented more than almost anything.

cards.title: Indecision costs you respect faster than tough choices do
cards.body:
Machiavelli says a leader becomes despised when seen as fickle, frivolous or irresolute. He should instead show courage, seriousness and strength, and make his decisions final, so no one hopes to talk him round or deceive him.

You don't need to be rigid to use this. People lose confidence in a parent, manager or team captain who changes position with every complaint. Take time to decide well, explain your reasons, and then stand by the decision unless genuinely new facts appear.
cards.quote: let him show that his judgments are irrevocable, and maintain himself in such reputation that no one can hope either to deceive him or to get round him.
cards.locator: XIX. That One Should Avoid Being Despised… ¶3
cards.apply_it: Think of a decision you keep reopening. Gather what you need, decide by a set date, and then tell people it's settled.

quiz.question: What makes a leader despised, according to Machiavelli?
options: Making firm, well-reasoned decisions
Showing courage in hard times
Being seen as fickle and irresolute
Taking advice from wise counsellors
quiz.explanation: He lists being fickle, frivolous and irresolute as qualities that make a leader contemptible.

cards.title: A divided team falls quickly under pressure
cards.body:
Some rulers of Machiavelli's time kept their towns split into rival factions so they would be easier to control. Machiavelli rejects this. When a real threat arrives, he says, a divided city is quickly lost, because the weaker side will help the outsiders.

Some managers still play staff off against each other or let feuds simmer because it keeps people busy competing. It may look manageable in calm times, but in a crisis a split team cannot pull together. Deal with rivalries openly and build shared goals instead.
cards.quote: when the enemy comes upon you in divided cities you are quickly lost, because the weakest party will always assist the outside forces
cards.locator: XX. Are Fortresses, and Many Other Things… ¶3
cards.apply_it: Is there an ongoing rivalry in your team or family? Bring the people together this week around one goal they share.

quiz.question: Why did Machiavelli reject keeping cities divided into factions?
options: Factions are too expensive to fund
It made the people too loyal to the prince
Factions only work in wartime
In a crisis a divided city is quickly lost
quiz.explanation: He says when an enemy comes, divided cities fall quickly because the weaker faction helps the outsiders.

cards.title: Former doubters can become your most loyal supporters
cards.body:
Machiavelli notes that new rulers often found more faithfulness in people they first distrusted than in those they trusted from the start. Those who began on the other side know they must prove themselves through actions, so they work harder, while comfortable supporters may grow careless.

In a new job or role, don't write off the people who were sceptical of you. Give them a fair chance and a real task. Many will become your strongest allies, precisely because they want to show your first impression of them was wrong.
cards.quote: they know it to be very necessary for them to cancel by deeds the bad impression which he had formed of them
cards.locator: XX. Are Fortresses, and Many Other Things… ¶5
cards.apply_it: Identify one person who doubted you at the start. Offer them a meaningful responsibility and see how they respond.

quiz.question: Why might people who first opposed a new leader serve him well?
options: They want to cancel the bad impression through their deeds
They are paid more than others
They have no other skills
They secretly want to replace him
quiz.explanation: Machiavelli says they work to undo the bad impression by deeds, while trusted supporters may grow careless.

cards.title: Sitting on the fence often leaves you with no friends
cards.body:
Machiavelli argues that a leader is respected when he clearly takes a side. Staying neutral in a fight between powerful neighbours usually backfires: the winner sees you as an unreliable friend, and the loser feels you abandoned him. He notes that the one who is not your friend asks you to stay neutral, while a true friend asks you to stand with him.

Not every dispute needs your involvement. But when people you depend on face a real test, refusing to commit can cost you both relationships. Choose thoughtfully, then commit.
cards.quote: he who is not your friend will demand your neutrality, whilst he who is your friend will entreat you to declare yourself
cards.locator: XXI. How a Prince Should Conduct Himself So… ¶4
cards.apply_it: Is there a situation where you are avoiding taking a stand to keep everyone happy? Decide where you honestly stand.

quiz.question: What happens to the neutral party, according to Machiavelli?
options: Both sides reward him equally
Neither the winner nor the loser treats him as a friend
He always becomes the strongest power
He is ignored and left completely safe
quiz.explanation: The winner distrusts a doubtful friend and the loser will not shelter someone who did not help.

cards.title: There is no perfectly safe option, so choose the lesser evil
cards.body:
Machiavelli warns that no one should imagine they can choose a completely safe course. In ordinary affairs, escaping one problem usually lands you in another. Wisdom is the ability to judge which troubles are worse, and pick the smaller one.

This frees you from waiting for a risk-free choice that never comes. Staying in a job has risks; leaving it has others. Instead of asking 'which option is safe?', ask 'which risks can I best live with and manage?' Then act.
cards.quote: prudence consists in knowing how to distinguish the character of troubles, and for choice to take the lesser evil.
cards.locator: XXI. How a Prince Should Conduct Himself So… ¶6
cards.apply_it: For a decision you're stuck on, list the main risk of each option. Pick the one whose risk you can best handle.

quiz.question: According to Machiavelli, what does prudence consist of?
options: Always finding a perfectly safe option
Avoiding all decisions until risks vanish
Telling troubles apart and choosing the lesser evil
Letting others decide for you
quiz.explanation: He says no course is perfectly safe; prudence is distinguishing troubles and choosing the lesser one.

cards.title: You don't need every idea yourself if you can judge others' ideas well
cards.body:
Machiavelli describes three kinds of minds: one that understands things on its own, one that recognises good thinking when others offer it, and one that does neither. The first is excellent, the second good, and the third useless.

This is encouraging. You don't have to be the most original person in the room to lead well. If you can tell good advice from bad, praise what is right and correct what is wrong, you can make excellent decisions and keep people honest. Developing that judgement is a skill anyone can practise.
cards.quote: there are three classes of intellects: one which comprehends by itself; another which appreciates what others comprehended; and a third which neither comprehends by itself nor by the showing of others
cards.locator: XXII. Concerning the Secretaries of Princes ¶2
cards.apply_it: Next time someone suggests an idea, pause to weigh its strengths and weaknesses out loud before accepting or rejecting it.

quiz.question: In Machiavelli's three kinds of minds, which is called 'good'?
options: The one that understands nothing at all
The one that ignores all advice
The one that copies whatever is popular
The one that recognises good thinking from others
quiz.explanation: The first understands on its own (excellent), the second appreciates what others understand (good), the third neither (useless).

cards.title: Trust people who put the shared work ahead of their own gain
cards.body:
Machiavelli offers one test for judging an assistant that he says never fails: if you see someone always thinking of his own interests before yours and seeking profit in everything, you will never be able to trust him.

When choosing a business partner, employee or treasurer for your group, watch how people handle small things. Do they quietly take the best for themselves, or care about the shared goal? Self-interest is normal, but someone who puts it first in every situation should not be trusted with what matters to you.
cards.quote: when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours, and seeking inwardly his own profit in everything, such a man will never make a good servant
cards.locator: XXII. Concerning the Secretaries of Princes ¶3
cards.apply_it: Before trusting someone with money or responsibility, recall two small situations where you saw whose interests they put first.

quiz.question: What is Machiavelli's test for whether an assistant can be trusted?
options: Whether he thinks more of his own interests than yours
Whether he comes from a noble family
Whether he agrees with everything you say
Whether he has worked for many princes
quiz.explanation: He says someone who seeks his own profit in everything will never be trustworthy.

cards.title: Leaders who consult no one end up changing course constantly
cards.body:
Machiavelli describes the Emperor Maximilian, who shared his plans with no one and took no advice. When his plans became known in action, the people around him objected, and he gave way. The result: what he did one day he undid the next, and nobody could rely on his decisions.

Keeping everything to yourself can feel strong, but it means your plans are tested only after you have committed. Consulting good people early, then deciding, leads to plans that last and a team that knows what you want.
cards.quote: those things he does one day he undoes the next, and no one ever understands what he wishes or intends to do, and no one can rely on his resolutions.
cards.locator: XXIII. How Flatterers Should Be Avoided ¶3
cards.apply_it: Before your next important decision, share the plan with two trusted people and ask what could go wrong.

quiz.question: Why did the Emperor Maximilian keep reversing his decisions?
options: He listened to too many advisers at once
He consulted no one, so his plans met objections only once in motion
He had no money to carry them out
He was forced out by foreign kings
quiz.explanation: Being secretive, his plans were challenged only when carried out, and being pliant, he kept abandoning them.

cards.title: Advice is only as good as the judgement of the person using it
cards.body:
Machiavelli warns against thinking a weak leader can simply rely on good advisers. Each adviser has his own interests, and a leader without judgement cannot weigh or combine their views. So, he concludes, good advice comes from a wise leader, not the other way round.

You can't fully outsource your thinking about your money, health choices or career. Experts and friends are valuable, but you still need enough understanding to ask good questions, spot conflicts of interest and make the final call.
cards.quote: good counsels, whencesoever they come, are born of the wisdom of the prince, and not the wisdom of the prince from good counsels.
cards.locator: XXIII. How Flatterers Should Be Avoided ¶6
cards.apply_it: Before your next big decision based on advice, learn enough basics to explain the choice in your own words.

quiz.question: Why can a leader without judgement not simply rely on advisers?
options: Advisers are always dishonest
Advice is never useful
He cannot weigh or unite their competing views
Advisers refuse to speak to weak leaders
quiz.explanation: Each adviser thinks of his own interests, and only a leader with judgement can weigh them.

cards.title: The approach that made you successful can later ruin you
cards.body:
Machiavelli explains why people prosper one day and fail the next without changing at all: the times change and they don't. A cautious person does well in cautious times but fails when boldness is needed, partly because temperament is hard to change, and partly because having always succeeded one way, he cannot believe another way is better.

Notice your default style, whether careful, fast, frugal or adventurous. Then ask honestly whether your current situation still rewards it.
cards.quote: having always prospered by acting in one way, he cannot be persuaded that it is well to leave it
cards.locator: XXV. What Fortune Can Effect in Human… ¶5
cards.apply_it: Write down the approach that has worked best for you so far. Then name one current situation where it may no longer fit.

quiz.question: Why do people often fail to adapt when the times change?
options: They never had any success before
They change their methods too often
Fortune always punishes the cautious
Past success with one method makes them reluctant to leave it
quiz.explanation: Machiavelli says nature resists change, and past success convinces people their old way is still best.

cards.title: Individual talent wins little without good leadership
cards.body:
Looking at Italian armies of his day, Machiavelli notes that Italians excelled in individual duels and small fights, but armies made of them performed poorly. The reason, he says, was weak leadership: the capable would not obey, and everyone thought he knew best.

Many teams today are full of skilled people who still underperform. Talent needs coordination: a clear direction, agreed roles and someone whose lead others accept. If your group is brilliant individually but stuck, the missing piece may be leadership, not ability.
cards.quote: Here there is great valour in the limbs whilst it fails in the head.
cards.locator: XXVI. An Exhortation to Liberate Italy from… ¶7
cards.apply_it: In a group you belong to, check: does everyone know the goal and their role? If not, propose a short meeting to agree on both.

quiz.question: Why did Italian armies perform poorly despite skilled individual fighters?
options: Weak leadership: the capable would not obey and each thought he knew best
The soldiers lacked strength and skill
They had too many good generals
They were always outnumbered
quiz.explanation: Machiavelli blames the leaders: valour in the limbs but failure in the head.
